title: Umm Amr made up her mind and left
intro: Al-Mufaddal al-Dabbi included this ode by al-Shanfara in his anthology. It opens with Umm Amr already on her way, yet the poet remembers the smallest particulars of how she walked and how she fed a neighbour. His account of travelling on foot introduces a second keeper of a household, the comrade responsible for feeding the band, whom the old commentary identifies as Ta'abbata Sharran. Recalling his feud with Salaman and his life away from his kin, he ends by stating what another person can expect of him.

translation: Umm Amr made up her mind and left.
She did not bid her neighbours farewell as she went.
1.sharh: Her decision and its execution come in two quick verbs. By the time the neighbours know she means to leave, the farewell they might have exchanged has been lost.

translation: Umm Amr got ahead of us with her plans.
Already she loomed above us on the riding camels.
2.sharh: The speaker learns her intention from the sight of the saddled camels and their towering necks. All the preparation must already have taken place.

translation: Before my very eyes she passed evening, night and morning.
She settled her affairs, rose to leave, and was gone.
3.sharh: He had every opportunity to see what she was doing. The long roll of time makes the short sequence of actions at the end sound all the more final.

translation: My liver aches for Umayma, after all
my hopes. Count her a blessing life let slip.
4.sharh: The cry names the liver, a seat of feeling in the old idiom. Calling her Umayma makes the attempt to reconcile himself to her loss especially tender.

translation: My neighbour, you have done nothing to earn blame.
When she is spoken of, no one finds cause for dislike.
5.sharh: He addresses her as though she could hear him, then speaks of her as the neighbours might. His hurt at her departure gives him no reason to fault her conduct.

translation: What pleased me was how her veil would never slip
when she walked, how she never glanced about.
6.sharh: He recalls two motions precisely because neither occurs. The veil stays in place and her gaze keeps its course.

translation: A little after people sleep, she takes her evening milk
to her neighbour, when few gifts are going round.
7.sharh: The timing lets her give privately. The gift is her own evening portion, given at the very time when few households can afford gifts.

translation: She makes her house a place beyond reproach
when other houses stand open to disparagement.
8.sharh: Moral standing is imagined as a choice of dwelling place. Her household has a secure site beyond the reach of censure.

translation: As if she had lost something on the ground, she follows it
straight ahead. When she speaks to you, her words are few.
9.sharh: A passer-by might think she was tracing a dropped object. When she does speak, her words are as measured as her gaze.

translation: No report of Umayma brings shame upon her husband.
When women are mentioned, she stands pure and honoured.
10.sharh: Reputation leaves the household and returns to it. What other people say when her name comes up gives her husband no cause to flinch.

translation: At evening he comes home to the delight of his eyes,
as a happy man returns, never asking where she spent the day.
11.sharh: The line registers trust through something the husband never feels the need to ask. Coming home gives pleasure untroubled by suspicion.

translation: Slender here and full there, tall and beautifully formed.
If beauty could make a human a jinni, it would make her one.
12.sharh: The first half keeps every proportion distinct. The second reaches beyond human beauty. The verb suggests possession by a jinn, and one old reading makes the woman herself seem otherworldly.

translation: We passed the night as though the house were enclosed above us
in basil stirred by wind at dusk and beaded with dew.
13.sharh: Scent has become the very roof of the house. Breeze and dew keep it fresh throughout the remembered night.

translation: Basil flowering in the bed of Halya valley,
fragrant, with no drought around it.
14.sharh: The imagined plant now grows in a particular valley. Its soil has escaped drought, so the remembered fragrance has a source as well as a name.

translation: Many a band with red bows I have roused.
A raider may gain spoils one day and give enemies joy another.
15.sharh: Weather and handling have coloured the bows. Before giving the expedition any outcome, he leaves open the chance that it will be the enemy's turn to rejoice.

translation: We left the valley between Mish'al
and al-Jaba. Far off indeed I set my company going.
16.sharh: Naming the valley's two landmarks fixes the point of departure. The interjection then asks the mind to span the distance the company has covered.

translation: I make my way on foot across ground that cannot hurt me,
to hurt a people or come upon my appointed end.
17.sharh: Confidence about the ground underfoot gives way to two possible outcomes. In the first he acts. In the second his own allotted death is waiting for him.

translation: I walk through the weariness and length of the expedition.
Each evening's going and each morning's brings me closer.
18.sharh: Evening and morning become measures of distance as well as time. The slow accumulation of walking answers the vastness announced in the valley.

translation: I have seen a mother of dependants apportion their food.
When she fed them, she gave out little and kept it scant.
19.sharh: The old commentary identifies this “mother” as his male companion Ta'abbata Sharran. Entrusted with everybody's provisions, he has the job and the anxieties of a parent.

translation: She fears want for us if she gives us more,
while we go hungry. How strictly she tends us.
20.sharh: Their hunger is real, as is the keeper's fear of worse hunger ahead. The exclamation of admiration has room for a hungry man's complaint.

translation: She has no wish to hoard what her bag contains.
It is fear of hunger that has made her save it.
21.sharh: He distinguishes between the contents of the bag and the reason they stay there. Today's withheld portion belongs to the same travellers tomorrow.

translation: She keeps company with outlaws. No curtain shuts her in.
Who expects her home unless she turns back from a raid?
22.sharh: The old commentary takes the last words to mean that the band can expect its companion at home only on a return from a raid. Another interpretation makes the travellers’ own chance of a night’s rest depend on her decision.

translation: She carries a quiver that yields thirty shafts.
At the first sight of the running men she bristles.
23.sharh: The same figure who watched over the food carries a full quiver. The body reacts to the approaching runners before there is time to speak.

translation: She approaches the runners with half a shin bare,
wheeling like the wild ass that looks back at its herd.
24.sharh: A hitched-up garment and a bared shin indicate urgency. The wild stallion keeps turning, alert to danger and to the animals in his charge.

translation: When they start in alarm she flies to a bright blade.
She casts what her quiver holds, then draws steel.
25.sharh: The pace quickens through a small series of verbs. The female pronoun still belongs to the band's “mother” as the sword comes into view.

translation: A keen sword the colour of salt, its iron clear,
a cutter like bright patches of a much-praised pool.
26.sharh: Salt gives the metal its whiteness. Separate gleams on a pool supply the changing light along the same hard surface.

translation: You see them like calves' tails as they leave the water,
having drunk once of blood and drunk again.
27.sharh: The plural points to the blades. The old commentary sees the calves whisk their tails at the sight of their mothers. The blades have been drinking too, and the poet names what they drank.

translation: We killed a pilgrim bearing an offering to avenge one with matted hair,
at Mina's stone heaps among the chanting pilgrims.
28.sharh: One pilgrim is described by his offering, the other by his prepared hair. The old account connects them with the father's death. The poet makes the crowd's ritual cry audible around the killing.

translation: We repaid Salaman son of Mufrij the debt
for what their hands had sent before and done amiss.
29.sharh: Salaman is an ancestor's name standing for his descendants. The language of a loan makes inherited violence sound like a debt that falls due.

translation: A people were congratulated on having me, though I did them no good.
I came to live among people I never wished for.
30.sharh: The welcome and the newcomer fail each other's expectations. An old account connects the first half with the boy being taken as a pledge, one fragment in conflicting traditions about his upbringing.

translation: Through Abd Allah we cooled some of our burning thirst,
and through Awf, where the charge began and voices rose.
31.sharh: Two names make the feud personal. Even here the speaker claims only partial relief from thirst, and the onset of battle is marked by a rising sound.

translation: When my death comes I shall give it no heed.
My mother's sisters and my father's sister will shed no tears.
32.sharh: Naming the women on either side of his family makes the missing mourners distinct. He imagines a death as far from the protection of kin as his life has been.

translation: Even had I never stirred from my family's tent,
my appointed end would have found me between its two poles.
33.sharh: The space between the poles is as far inside a home as one can get. Death could have found him even there.

translation: If I complain of want, spare me the sickbed visit.
My run high in Dhu al-Burayqayn cured me.
34.sharh: The speaker treats poverty like an illness for which a friend might visit. His own remedy is the run into the hills. In the Cairo version the early start itself brings relief.

translation: I am sweet if anyone seeks my sweetness,
and bitter when my wary spirit turns bitter.
35.sharh: Sweetness and bitterness let two people determine the flavour of an encounter. The repeated sounds for “bitter” and “turn bitter” bring the response close to its cause.

translation: What I refuse, I refuse absolutely. Yet swift is my return
to anyone who sets their heart on giving me joy.
36.sharh: His refusals are decisive, but his return need take no time at all. The man first seen losing a neighbour ends by telling others how readily they can win him back.

1.1.2-3.head: أُمّ عَمرٍو
1.1.2-3.meaning: Umm Amr, the beloved's kunya. A few lines later he calls her Umayma.

1.1.4.head: أَجمَعَ
1.1.4.meaning: Made up her mind and resolved on a course of action.

2.2.4.head: أَظَلَّ
2.2.4.meaning: Loomed over the onlooker from the back of her mount.

3.1.1.meaning: “Before my two eyes.” He witnesses the hours passing yet misses her plan.

3.2.1.head: قَضّى
3.2.1.meaning: Finished off the several things she needed to do.

4.1.1-2.head: وا كَبِدا
4.1.1-2.meaning: “Oh, my liver.” A cry of grief naming an organ associated with feeling. The opening sound before the lament is indistinct.

4.2.2.head: هَب
4.2.2.meaning: “Count her as.” An invitation to regard her as a blessing once enjoyed.

5.1.5.head: مُليمَة
5.1.5.meaning: Having given real occasion for blame.

5.2.5.head: تَقَلّى
5.2.5.meaning: To make oneself disliked. The old commentary hears an echo of what people might say of another woman. Umayma gives them no cause to say it.

6.1.5.head: قِناع
6.1.5.meaning: A woman's head-covering, which stays in place with her measured walk.

7.1.5.head: غَبوق
7.1.5.meaning: The milk set aside for the evening drink.

8.1.2.head: مَنجاة
8.1.2.meaning: A place of safety beyond the reach of harm.

9.1.5.head: نِسي
9.1.5.meaning: A small possession left behind or dropped.

9.1.6.head: قَصَّ
9.1.6.meaning: Trace or follow as one follows a track.

9.2.2.head: أَمّ
9.2.2.meaning: Her course, the direction she means to keep.

9.2.5.head: بَلَتَ
9.2.5.meaning: Cut short or keep brief, here of her reply.

10.1.4.head: نَثا
10.1.4.meaning: What gets said or passed from mouth to mouth about someone.

10.1.5.head: حَليل
10.1.5.meaning: Her husband, the man who shares her home.

11.1.5-6.head: قُرَّة العَين
11.1.5-6.meaning: “Coolness of his eye.” The person whose sight brings contentment.

11.2.6.head: ظَلَّ
11.2.6.meaning: Spent the daylight hours in a place.

12.1.3.head: اِسبَكَرَّ
12.1.3.meaning: Grew tall and straight in figure.

12.2.6.head: جُنَّ
12.2.6.meaning: Possessed by a jinn or transported beyond ordinary human appearance. The image admits more than one reading.

13.1.4.meaning: Enclosed on all sides, as with a surrounding structure.

13.2.4.head: طُلَّ
13.2.4.meaning: Moistened with dew or a fine fall of moisture.

14.1.4.head: حَليَة
14.1.4.meaning: Halya, a wadi associated with the Sarat highlands.

14.2.6.head: مُسنِت
14.2.6.meaning: Overtaken by a year of drought.

15.1.1.head: باضِعَة
15.1.1.meaning: A detachment or band that has broken away from the larger group.

15.2.5.head: شُمِتَ بِهِ
15.2.5.meaning: Give one's enemies occasion to exult over a reverse.

16.1.6.head: مِشعَل
16.1.6.meaning: Mish'al, one landmark used to place the valley of departure.

16.2.2.meaning: Al-Jaba, the other landmark defining the valley.

16.2.5.head: سُربَة
16.2.5.meaning: The band travelling in company with him.

17.2.1.head: نَكى
17.2.1.meaning: To inflict hurt or loss upon an adversary.

17.2.5.head: حُمَّة
17.2.5.meaning: One's allotted destiny, especially the appointed death.

18.1.3.head: أَين
18.1.3.meaning: Weariness or exhaustion, a noun here.

19.1.1-2.head: أُمّ عِيال
19.1.1-2.meaning: “Mother of dependants.” The band's name here for its keeper of provisions, identified as Ta'abbata Sharran.

20.1.3.head: العَيل
20.1.3.meaning: Destitution, here the danger of running out of food.

20.2.3-5.head: أَيَّ آلٍ تَأَلَّت
20.2.3-5.meaning: “What tending she gave them.” An old expression of wonder at their stern management.

21.1.4.head: ضِنّ
21.1.4.meaning: Stinginess, an unwillingness to part with what one holds.

22.1.1.head: مُصَعلِكَة
22.1.1.meaning: One who lives with the outlaws, in the feminine idiom of the nickname.

22.2.6.head: بَيَّتَ
22.2.6.meaning: Make a night expedition. Commentators also understand the line of a return from one.

23.1.5.head: سَيحَف
23.1.5.meaning: An arrow described as broad-headed or finely pointed in the old glosses.

23.2.4.head: العَدِيّ
23.2.4.meaning: A group of running men, here those approaching from the opposing side.

24.2.2-3.head: عَير العانَة
24.2.2-3.meaning: “The herd's stallion.” A male wild ass on the watch over his jennies.

26.2.1.head: جُراز
26.2.1.meaning: A blade with a keen cutting edge.

26.2.4.head: المُنَعَّت
26.2.4.meaning: Often described or praised, here a pool famed for its clear surface.

27.1.4.head: صادِر
27.1.4.meaning: Returning from the watering place after drinking.

28.1.3.head: مُهدٍ
28.1.3.meaning: A pilgrim bringing an animal for an offering.

28.1.4.head: مُلَبِّد
28.1.4.meaning: In return for a pilgrim whose hair had been matted down for consecration.

28.2.1-2.head: جِمار مِنى
28.2.1-2.meaning: The places of ritual stoning at Mina, close to Mecca.

29.1.2-4.head: سَلامان اِبن مُفرِج
29.1.2-4.meaning: Salaman ibn Mufrij, the ancestor whose name designates the Azd clan in the feud.

29.2.4.head: أَزَلَّ
29.2.4.meaning: Brought about an offence or let it proceed from their hands.

30.2.5.head: مُنيَة
30.2.5.meaning: My wish or desire. Another transmission has “my stock”, the people of my birth.

31.1.5.head: غَليل
31.1.5.meaning: A burning thirst, here the persistent longing for requital.

31.2.3.meaning: The place of the charge or encounter.

33.1.3.head: رامَ
33.1.3.meaning: Stir from one's place or leave it.

34.1.6.head: خَلَّة
34.1.6.meaning: Need or poverty. A differently vocalised form means friendship.

34.2.3-4.head: ذو البُرَيقَين
34.2.3-4.meaning: Dhu al-Burayqayn, the place where he locates his restorative run.

35.2.4.head: العَزوف
35.2.4.meaning: A disposition quick to turn away from what displeases it.

36.1.5.head: مَباءَة
36.1.5.meaning: A return after withdrawal or estrangement.

36.2.4.head: اِنتَحى
36.2.4.meaning: Aim or set one's mind deliberately towards something.

23.1.3.meaning: The thirty shafts form part of its equipment. Both Cairo and Lyall read fiha, “in it”.

34.2.5.head: عَدوَة
34.2.5.meaning: My run on foot. Lyall prints this form. The Cairo edition has ghudwati, “my early start”.

5.2.2.head: ذُكِرَ
5.2.2.meaning: When she is mentioned. The speaker briefly turns from addressing Umayma to talking about her. Lyall prints a third-person feminine verb.

34.1.2-3.meaning: “Do not visit me.” The verb is used for calling on a sick person, which prepares for the word “cured” in the next half.

4.1.4.head: أُمَيمَة
4.1.4.meaning: Umayma, the Umm Amr of the opening. Abd Allah al-Tayyib hears the change from her formal name to the diminutive as a sign of longing.

31.1.2-3.head: عَبدُ اللَّه
31.1.2-3.meaning: Abd Allah, identified by al-Anbari as a man of Salaman ibn Mufrij against whom the band took vengeance.

31.2.1.head: عَوف
31.2.1.meaning: Awf, another man of Salaman killed with Abd Allah in the old account. The poet claims only a measure of relief at their deaths.
